## Introduction

We will be studying 2025 NFL 4th Quarter Red Zone offenses by creating a logistic regression model that predicts the probability of the pass. This is a particularly interesting topic because the NFL has experienced recent change when it comes to Red Zone offensive success. According to Sports Info Solutions, Red Zone success rate hit a ten year low in 2024. This was primarily caused by a historically low Red Zone Passing success rate, as rushing success rates have remained mostly stable over the last ten years. We suspect that this trend may have changed play calling decisions during the 2025 season. Furthermore, in retrospect the NFL did indeed see general changes in play calling during the 2025 season. Teams shifted towards heavier sets (12+ personnel), with the Seahawks, the eventual Super Bowl Champions, and Rams, the NFC runners-up, leading the charge (ESPN). 13 personnel specifically experienced the most growth in 2025 (PFF). This is particularly interesting, however, as the actual efficiency, by EPA, of the formation did not increase from 2024 to 2025 (Sharp Football Analysis). These trends indicate the importance of personnel is predicting the pre-snap probability of the snap.

## Data Summary

This section describes where our data came from and summarizes its key features. The data contain 150 fourth-quarter red zone plays from the 2025 NFL season, each labeled as a drop back or a designed run. We first describe how the data were collected and what we changed, then summarize the relationships between each predictor and the response using the plots in Appendix C, and finally assess multicollinearity and screen variables.

### Metadata Description

### EDA Summary

The response, dropback, is binary, so logistic regression is appropriate. Of the 150 plays, 76 (50.7%) were drop backs and 74 (49.3%) were designed runs (Appendix C, response bar plot), so the classes are nearly perfectly balanced. The model will have 10 coefficients (5 quantitative predictors, 2 for personnel, 2 for down_group, and 1 for crunch_time). That gives about 7.4 events per predictor (74/10), so we will be cautious about overfitting and consider dropping weak predictors during screening. Plays from the same team and game may not be fully independent, which we treat as a limitation.

Personnel shows the clearest relationship with the response. The drop back rate was 59.3% (54 of 91) for 11_Light, 39.4% (13 of 33) for 12, and 34.6% (9 of 26) for heavy (Appendix C, personnel mosaic plot). The drop back rate falls as tight ends are added, as we expected. 11_Light makes up 60.7% of plays, while heavy has only 26 plays, so its estimate will be less precise.

Offenses that dropped back were typically trailing, while offenses that ran were typically even or ahead. The mean lead was -6.59 points on drop backs (median -10, IQR -17 to 7) versus +0.77 on runs (median 0, IQR -6.75 to 7.75) (Appendix C, boxplot). This supports a negative relationship between lead and drop back probability. The sample is split between 55 plays trailing by 9+, 39 trailing by 1 to 8 or tied, 24 leading by 1 to 8, and 32 leading by 9+. Offense spread shows a similar but weaker pattern, with mean spread of -0.38 on drop backs versus +1.41 on runs, so underdogs passed somewhat more.

The drop back rate was 48.3% on 1st down (29 of 60), 42.0% on 2nd (21 of 50), and 65.0% on 3rd/4th (26 of 40) (Appendix C, down mosaic plot). Later downs are associated with more passing, but 2nd down is not higher than 1st. Distance moves in the same direction: mean ydstogo was 7.18 on drop backs versus 6.55 on runs (medians 8 and 6.5). The first quartile differs most (4.75 vs 3), consistent with short-yardage runs.

crunch_time shows no marginal relationship, with drop back rates of 50.5% (46 of 91) outside crunch time and 50.8% (30 of 59) inside it. The team success-rate variables separate the classes only slightly. Mean dropback_sr was 45.35 on drop backs versus 46.58 on runs, and mean rush_sr was 41.99 versus 42.64. These likely carry little signal, and they are the best candidates to drop in screening.

Two of the three interaction plots show clearly non-parallel lines (though cell sizes are small, see below):
- Lead × crunch time: The effect of crunch time depends on the lead, even though crunch time has no marginal effect. Offenses leading by 9+ dropped back about 35% of the time before crunch time but only about 13% during it (clock-killing runs). Offenses trailing by 9+ went the other way, from about 72% to 82%. The lines cross, which supports including this term.
- Distance × down: On 2nd down, drop back rate climbs steeply with distance (about 20% at 1 to 3 yards to over 70% at 10+). On 3rd/4th down, it is highest at 7 to 9 yards (about 88%), and the 10+ yard group drops to about 60%.
- Personnel × distance: 11_Light is relatively flat across distance, while 12 rises with distance. The heavy line is jagged because each distance bin holds only a handful of plays, so we don’t read much into it.

We assessed multicollinearity using variance inflation factors from the full model. All adjusted GVIF values were between 1.04 and 1.36, well below the  cutoff. The strongest pairwise relationship was between score differential and offense spread (r ≈ 0.62), which is expected since favored teams tend to lead, but it did not inflate the variances enough to be a concern. Therefore, no variables were removed due to multicollinearity.

From the iterative process, game situation, especially score differential, is the strongest predictor of whether a red zone offense dropped back in the fourth quarter of the 2025 season. Offenses that were trailing passed significantly more, while later downs and lighter personnel were associated with more passing in the expected direction, but these effects were not statistically conclusive with 150 plays.

```{r, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE,results=FALSE}
## Use this code chunk can be used to execute any functions or summaries
## that will not be included in your output such as correlations or 5 number summaries

# Full model
model <- glm(
  dropback ~ ydstogo + score_differential + dropback_sr + rush_sr +
    offense_spread + crunch_time + personnel + down_group,
  data = RedZone,
  family = binomial
)

# Calculate VIF
vif(model)

step(model, direction = "backward")
```

### Appendix C: Exploratory Data Analysis

```{r, echo=FALSE}
## Use this code  to include the relevant plots from EDA
## This should NOT be a dump of all of your plots and outputs.
## Refer to the Rmarkdown guide for sizing information on your plots

# This partition is optional, but can be useful for a simple way to resize your plots
par(mfrow=c(2,3),pin=c(1,1),mar=c(7.1,4.1,3,1))

#Quantitative - ydstogo
boxplot(ydstogo~dropback, data=RedZone)
tapply(RedZone$ydstogo,RedZone$dropback,summary)

#Quantitative - score differential
boxplot(score_differential~dropback, data=RedZone)
tapply(RedZone$score_differential,RedZone$dropback,summary)

#Quantitative - offense spread
boxplot(offense_spread~dropback, data=RedZone)
tapply(RedZone$offense_spread,RedZone$dropback,summary)

#Quantitative - dropback success rate
boxplot(dropback_sr~dropback, data=RedZone)
tapply(RedZone$dropback_sr,RedZone$dropback,summary)

#Quantitative - rush success rate
boxplot(rush_sr~dropback, data=RedZone)
tapply(RedZone$rush_sr,RedZone$dropback,summary)

#Qualitative - personnel
RedZone$personnel<-factor(RedZone$personnel)
levels(RedZone$personnel)<-c("11_Light","12", "heavy")
mosaicplot(dropback~personnel,data=RedZone)
table(RedZone$personnel,RedZone$dropback)
prop.table(table(RedZone$personnel,RedZone$dropback),margin=2)

#Qualitative - down_group
RedZone$down_group<-factor(RedZone$down_group)
levels(RedZone$down_group)<-c("1st","2nd", "3rd_4th")
mosaicplot(dropback~down_group,data=RedZone)
table(RedZone$down_group,RedZone$dropback)
prop.table(table(RedZone$down_group,RedZone$dropback),margin=2)

#Qualitative - crunch_time
RedZone$crunch_time<-factor(RedZone$crunch_time)
mosaicplot(dropback~crunch_time,data=RedZone)
table(RedZone$crunch_time,RedZone$dropback)
prop.table(table(RedZone$crunch_time,RedZone$dropback),margin=2)

#Binning
RedZone$ydstogo_group <- cut(RedZone$ydstogo, breaks=c(0,3,6,9,Inf), labels=c("1-3 yds","4-6 yds","7-9 yds","10+ yds"))
RedZone$lead_group <- cut(RedZone$score_differential, breaks=c(-Inf,-9,0,8,Inf), labels=c("Trailing 9+","Trailing 1-8 / Tied","Leading 1-8","Leading 9+"))
table(RedZone$ydstogo_group)
table(RedZone$lead_group)

#Interaction - ydstogo and down_group
interaction.plot(RedZone$down_group, RedZone$ydstogo_group, RedZone$dropback, fun=mean, trace.label="Yards to Go"
                 , xlab="Down", ylab="Mean Dropback (Pass Rate)", main="Interaction Plot Yards to Go X Down")

#Interaction - score_differential and crunch_time
interaction.plot(RedZone$crunch_time, RedZone$lead_group, RedZone$dropback, fun=mean, trace.label="Lead"
                 , xlab="Crunch Time", ylab="Mean Dropback (Pass Rate)", main="Interaction Plot Lead X Crunch Time")

#Interaction - ydstogo and personnel
interaction.plot(RedZone$ydstogo_group, RedZone$personnel, RedZone$dropback, fun=mean, trace.label="Personnel"
                 , xlab="Yards to Go", ylab="Mean Dropback (Pass Rate)", main="Interaction Plot Personnel X Yards to Go")

#Response variable - dropback
barplot(table(RedZone$dropback), xlab="Play Type (0 = Run, 1 = Dropback)", ylab="Number of Plays", main="Distribution of Red Zone Play Calls")
```
